title: Do rework metrics find the defects in code written by AI coding agents?
lede: research programme testing repository-mining defect signals against audited defects in an agent-written repository: across 4,085 audited defect lines and 5,929 matched controls, no 14-day rework proxy (fix links, fix-touches, reverts) separates them, and defects sat on main a median 34 days before an audit found them.
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) on this repository studying itself. Every pull request here is written and merged by coding-agent sessions with no human review, and a quality track audits random samples of the work and names each defect’s file and line. Milestone 1 traces 4,085 audited defect lines (640 audits) with git blame to the 794 pull requests that wrote them and compares them with 5,929 random lines of the same files and trees. No rework proxy separates them: a later fix-worded PR naming the PR flags 2.6% of defect lines and 2.5% of controls (Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio 1.56, 95% CI 0.88–2.77), a fix-worded PR touching the file within 14 days 24.0% against 20.2% (0.80, 0.60–1.07), and nothing was reverted. The median defect line had been on main 34 days when it was found, and 92% were older than the 14-day window rework metrics use. In 1,575 of 2,150 audited files one pull request wrote every sampled line, so no per-PR signal could localise the defect there. Limitations: the auditors are agent sessions with a rubric, line links fit omission defects badly (milestone 2 measures link validity), and it is one repository.
